Figure methods and captions

The conceptual framework is Figure 1. The empirical figures below follow the order used in the manuscript. Method summaries are working text and are kept separate from the publication-ready captions.

Figure 2 — Holocene climate change and fire

Method summary. Adjacent 1,000-year changes in spring temperature, winter temperature, summer precipitation, and winter precipitation were evaluated at ten 100-year phases and standardized by the corresponding standard deviations among the 607 matched legacy CCA calibration plots. The three MORA lake trajectories were averaged before MORA and NOCA received equal regional weight. A variable qualified when its absolute median regional change reached 50% of its maximum and at least eight phases supported its direction; any qualifying variable defined climate change. High-fire periods were classified independently from accepted charcoal-event frequencies normalized within core and aggregated by site, using a threshold of the site median plus 1.4826 × MAD. Anthropocene climate contrasts compare 1979–1989 with six season-years Y−5 through Y for each plot, where Y is the selected adult resurvey year. Midpoint intervals run from 1984 to Y−2.5: 27.5–32.5 years at MORA and 27.5–28.5 years at NOCA.

Figure 2. Holocene climate change and fire.

Publication-ready caption. Figure 2. Holocene climate-change eras and high-fire evidence at Mount Rainier (MORA) and North Cascades (NOCA). A. Signed 1,000-year changes in the four CCA climate variables, standardized by their pooled legacy-calibration standard deviations and summarized with equal weight for MORA and NOCA. Points mark variables meeting both the variable-specific magnitude threshold and the eight-of-ten phase-direction criterion. Background bands identify climate-change (CC) and climate-stability (S) eras; arrows show the direction of time, and CC1a–CC1c annotations describe the retained climate directions within CC1. Brackets at the older margin show the variable-specific standardized stability ranges. The inset compares the maximum-absolute Holocene regional median after ten-offset aggregation with median Anthropocene plot-level rates in physical units per century. The Anthropocene entries are annualized short-window contrasts: MORA compares 1979–1989 with each plot’s adult-year window Y−5 through Y over 27.5–32.5 midpoint years; NOCA uses the same rule over 27.5–28.5 midpoint years. The MORA precipitation contrast should be interpreted with the documented possible post-2010 CHELSA inhomogeneity. B. Site-specific charcoal event-frequency ratios relative to the robust high-fire threshold. The dashed line denotes a ratio of 1; red segments and points identify dates classified as high fire. Ages are calibrated years before present (cal BP; present = 1950).

Figure 3 — Observed and climate-predicted CCA trajectories

Method summary. A common canonical correspondence analysis (CCA) was fit to 14 retained taxa and four seasonal climate constraints in 607 matched legacy plots. Observed communities were represented by weighted-average (WA) scores and climate-predicted communities by linear-combination (LC) scores in the unchanged CCA1–CCA2, scaling-1 (scaling = "sites"), Hill-off geometry. Holocene positions are MORA and NOCA centroids within each frozen CC1–S4 era; Anthropocene positions are site means of the same 330 MORA and 277 NOCA valid paired plots at both legacy and resurvey dates, for both WA and LC. MORA uses the latest adult visit and its matching seedlings; modern climate uses Y−5 through Y for each selected adult survey year Y. All-zero retained-taxon rows are excluded from both sides of these comparisons. Climate bars quantify each constraint’s unique marginal loss of constrained inertia, whereas species bars partition constrained inertia among taxa.

Figure 3. Observed and climate-predicted CCA trajectories.

Publication-ready caption. Figure 3. Observed and climate-predicted forest community trajectories in the common CCA space. A. Observed WA and climate-predicted LC trajectories for MORA and NOCA. Holocene paths connect site-level centroids chronologically from CC1 through S4; Anthropocene arrows connect legacy and resurvey means from identical valid pairs at both dates (330 MORA, 277 NOCA). Predicted paths and annotations are shown with reduced opacity. The grey points are legacy calibration plots; the panel is cropped to the trajectories; calibration plots outside the displayed extent remain in the model. B. CCA biplot showing the four climate vectors and species scores; all taxa are plotted, while names are shown only for species vectors at least 25% as long as the longest species vector. C. Unique marginal effect of each climate constraint, expressed as a percentage of total constrained inertia. These values are not additive because the constraints share explanatory variation. D. Taxon-specific partition of constrained inertia; shading indicates occurrence in the 607 calibration plots.

Figure 4 — Era contrasts and corrected lag-change rates

Method summary. Offset-0 MA1 GLS results are reused without refitting for physical climate-change rate, observed community turnover and observed, pace-corrected and direction-corrected lag changes. Models use era * site, REML and separate era/site residual variances. Corrected rates are calculated within each chronology draw from stored counterfactual geometry before finite-draw transition medians. The original 23/21-column model tables are preserved. Contrast and group-mean intervals use Satterthwaite degrees of freedom; contrast SEs retain covariance between fitted means. Correlations are descriptive and nominal, without adjustment for lake/temporal dependence or mathematical coupling.

Figure 4. Offset-0 model contrasts and observed-versus-corrected lag changes.

Publication-ready caption. Figure 4. Holocene–Anthropocene comparisons at Mount Rainier (MORA, blue) and North Cascades (NOCA, orange). The upper row shows Anthropocene-minus-Holocene MA(1) GLS contrasts and 95% confidence intervals for standardized climate change per century, community turnover rate and observed lag change. Contrast dots, bars and numeric annotations identify MORA/NOCA in blue/orange; response labels are uncolored. Climate uses a separate scale from the CCA distance-per-century responses; zero baselines are aligned and both y-axes are on the left. * denotes unadjusted contrast p < 0.05; nonsignificant interval bars are faint, as are the dots and numeric annotations for nonsignificant NOCA contrasts. Numbers beneath intervals are ratios of fitted Anthropocene to Holocene means, without ratio intervals. Signed lag ratios may reflect sign reversals and become unstable near zero; they are descriptive annotations, not multiplicative-effect inference. Climate change is the Euclidean norm of four seasonal changes scaled by pooled legacy-calibration SDs per climate century. Turnover is observed CCA displacement per vegetation century. Observed lag change is the change in observed-to-predicted CCA distance per climate century; corrected rates substitute the maintained counterfactual final lag while preserving the actual initial lag. The lower row plots observed lag-change rate against lag-change rate after correction, both in CCA distance per century, separately for each era, pooling parks. Small transparent points retain park fills and correction outlines; colored straight lines are descriptive linear fits, dashed diagonals are 1:1, and colored text gives Spearman rho and nominal two-sided p values. Below 1:1, correction reduces final lag; above it, correction increases final lag; on it, final lag is unchanged. Grey annotations appear in the corresponding regions and along the 1:1 line in each scatter panel. Equal x/y distance scales keep the diagonal at 45°. This interpretation follows within each calculated transition from the shared initial lag and climate elapsed time. Holocene points compare response-specific chronology-draw medians, rather than directly summarizing the draw-level correction effects. Top densities show observed lag rates once per observation, with their original MA1 fitted means and 95% intervals. Holocene values are chronology-draw medians for actual offset-0 transitions: 20 MORA and 10 NOCA. Observed/direction modern values comprise 330 MORA and 277 NOCA pairs; pace retains 254 and 211, respectively, after excluding undefined stationary directions. The geometric corrections are descriptive, not causal, and model intervals do not propagate chronology uncertainty. Per-century units do not equalize temporal averaging across eras.

Separate corrected-lag contrast figure. The offset-0 pace- and direction-corrected lag-change contrasts are retained in their own PDF and embedded in the Analysis Review. The dots, bars and numeric annotations identify MORA/NOCA in blue/orange, while pink/purple x-axis labels identify the corrections. Intervals, stars, significance opacity and fold annotations follow the Figure 4 conventions. These contrasts reuse the existing MA1 results and are expressed in CCA distance per century.
